abstract.t: This document specifies Version 1 of the Oblivious Transport Security (OTS) protocol. OTS provides a connection-oriented, encrypted, and authenticated transport channel that operates independently of the underlying carrier network. Unlike TLS, OTS eliminates plaintext handshake metadata, client implementation fingerprints, traffic-analysis side channels, and cross-epoch network-layer address correlation by enforcing fixed-size datagrams, constant-rate transmission scheduling, cryptographic path binding, and synchronized ephemeral endpoint rotation without third-party proxies or relays.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: Conventional transport security protocols such as TLS 1.3 protect application-layer confidentiality and integrity but expose significant metadata to passive network observers. This metadata includes plaintext Server Name Indication (SNI) fields, cipher and extension preferences that fingerprint client implementations, variable packet lengths, inter-packet arrival timings that reveal application behavior and throughput, and persistent network-layer identifiers.

Oblivious Transport Security (OTS) eliminates these leaks natively at the transport layer without relying on third-party proxies, relays, or peer-to-peer forwarding networks. Every OTS datagram has an identical wire length, every endpoint uses a single mandatory cryptographic suite without feature negotiation, return delivery state is bound dynamically through cryptographic path validation, and endpoints transmit at deterministic intervals using indistinguishable cover frames when application data is absent.

section.name: Protocol Overview
section.t: OTS is a carrier-agnostic transport security protocol. While primarily deployed over UDP , OTS operates identically over any bidirectional datagram or byte-stream carrier -- including web endpoints, direct IPv6 sockets, local links, and peer-to-peer transports -- without requiring changes to the protocol state machine.

An OTS session consists of a single round-trip (1-RTT) cryptographic handshake followed by a bidirectional sequence of fixed-length frames. OTS decouples session identity and metadata protection entirely from the underlying carrier network, operating purely between the two communicating endpoints with zero third-party infrastructure.

To prevent implementation fingerprinting, OTS defines no version negotiation, no cipher-suite negotiation, and no optional handshake extensions. Any datagram deviating from the exact byte layout defined in MUST be silently discarded without generating an error response.

section.name: Wire Format
section.t: All OTS datagrams MUST be exactly 1280 octets in length, matching the IPv6 minimum link MTU to prevent network-layer fragmentation. Datagrams of any other length MUST be dropped.

ol.li: Version (Bytes 0 to 0 -- 1 octet): 8-bit unsigned integer. For this specification, the value MUST be 0x01.
Type (Bytes 1 to 1 -- 1 octet): 8-bit unsigned integer identifying the packet class: 0x01 for a Handshake Datagram, or 0x02 for a Protected Data Datagram.
Reserved (Bytes 2 to 3 -- 2 octets): 16-bit field. MUST be set to 0x0000 by the sender and verified as 0x0000 by the receiver.

Connection ID (Bytes 4 to 11 -- 8 octets): 64-bit opaque identifier. For initial Handshake Datagrams (Type 0x01), this field MUST contain a cryptographically random 64-bit value generated by the client.
Packet Number (Bytes 12 to 19 -- 8 octets): 64-bit monotonically increasing unsigned integer starting at 0. Used as the 96-bit AEAD nonce (left-padded with 32 zero bits).
Encrypted Payload (Bytes 20 to 1263 -- 1244 octets): Ciphertext encrypted under the active AEAD key. Upon decryption, the plaintext structure conforms to .
Authentication Tag (Bytes 1264 to 1279 -- 16 octets): 16-octet Poly1305 tag computed over the 1264-octet datagram prefix (header plus encrypted payload).

section.name: Decrypted Inner Frame Layout (1244 Octets Total)

ol.li: Frame Type (Byte 0 -- 1 octet): 0x00 for a Cover Frame, 0x01 for Stream Data, or 0x02 for Control and Acknowledgment.
Payload Length (Bytes 1 to 2 -- 2 octets): 16-bit unsigned integer in network byte order specifying valid octets in Frame Data (0 to 1241). For Cover Frames (0x00), this field MUST be 0.
Frame Data and Zero Padding (Bytes 3 to 1243 -- 1241 octets): Application or control bytes followed by zero padding. All octets beyond Payload Length MUST be set to 0x00 prior to encryption.

No alternative algorithms, cipher suites, or parameter sets are permitted.

section.name: Handshake Protocol
section.t: Prior to initiating a connection, the client obtains the server's static X25519 encryption key and Ed25519 verification key via an authenticated DNS SVCB/HTTPS resource record or out-of-band service configuration.

section.name: Client Initial (Flight 1)
section.t: The client generates an ephemeral X25519 key pair (ec_priv, ec_pub) and computes a shared secret with the server's static X25519 key. Using HKDF-SHA256, it derives an initial handshake key to encrypt the target Server Name Indication (SNI), a 64-bit Unix timestamp, and a 32-octet random anti-replay nonce. The client transmits ec_pub in cleartext within the first 32 octets of the payload area, followed by the AEAD ciphertext, padded to 1280 octets.

section.name: Server Response (Flight 2)
section.t: Upon valid AEAD verification, timestamp validation (within a +/- 30 second window), and anti-replay nonce check, the server binds the session's initial return delivery path to the authenticated source socket of Flight 1. The server generates an ephemeral X25519 key pair (es_priv, es_pub), computes the ephemeral shared secret, and derives bi-directional forward-secret traffic keys via HKDF-SHA256. The server signs the handshake transcript hash with its Ed25519 private key, encrypts the signature, an initial rotated Connection ID pool, and the session Tick Interval (T) under the derived traffic key, and transmits the 1280-octet response.

section.name: Isochronous Transmission
section.t: Once Flight 2 is processed, both endpoints MUST initialize a periodic timer set to Tick Interval T. At each tick expiration, the endpoint MUST emit exactly one 1280-octet Protected Data Datagram (Type 0x02).

If outbound application data is queued, the endpoint constructs a Stream Data frame (0x01). If no application data or control frames are queued, the endpoint MUST construct a Cover Frame (0x00). Both frame types undergo identical AEAD encryption and produce wire-indistinguishable datagrams.

section.name: Fingerprint Uniformity
section.t: Implementations MUST NOT vary packet sizes, padding bytes, handshake field ordering, or initial transmission parameters based on host operating system, application type, or user configuration.

section.name: Cryptographic Path Binding and Address Rotation
section.t: To prevent passive path observers from correlating endpoints via network-layer addresses without relying on intermediary relays or NAT-fragile static tokens, OTS binds session state exclusively to cryptographic identifiers and rotates carrier addresses dynamically.

section.name: Dynamic Cryptographic Path Binding
section.t: Responders MUST NOT treat network-layer IP addresses or transport ports as persistent client identifiers. Return delivery paths are bound solely upon verifying the ChaCha20-Poly1305 authentication tag of an incoming datagram carrying a valid active Connection ID. This allows OTS to traverse consumer NATs, carrier-grade NATs (CGNAT), and multi-homed interfaces seamlessly.

section.name: Synchronized Ephemeral Address Rotation
section.t: On carriers supporting dynamic address allocation (such as IPv6 temporary addresses ), an OTS initiator MUST maintain a rolling pool of ephemeral source addresses. At each Rotation Epoch (default: 256 datagrams or 10 seconds), the endpoint MUST atomically switch both its outbound source IP address and its active 64-bit Connection ID to an unused value pre-negotiated via encrypted Control Frames (0x02).

Upon verifying the AEAD tag of the first datagram arriving under the new Connection ID, the responder updates its return socket state to the new path. Because datagram size and transmission cadence remain invariant across transitions, passive path observers cannot link pre-rotation and post-rotation traffic flows.

section.name: Multi-Tenant Anycast Service Blinding
section.t: OTS responders SHOULD deploy behind shared Anycast IP prefixes. Service selection is bound exclusively to the encrypted SNI carried inside Flight 1 (), ensuring destination IP addresses do not identify specific hostnames or applications to on-path observers.

section.name: Security Considerations
section.t: OTS is a standalone, two-party transport protocol and does not rely on third-party proxies, relays, or peer-to-peer forwarding networks. Transport metadata, implementation fingerprints, transmission rates, and cross-epoch network address correlation are mitigated natively between the communicating endpoints.

Within a single Rotation Epoch, an on-path observer located directly on the physical link between initiator and responder can observe the active ephemeral carrier address pair for that window; however, synchronized ephemeral address and Connection ID rotation prevents persistent tracking or session reconstruction across epochs.

Replay attacks on Flight 1 are mitigated via timestamp window enforcement and a server-side cache of seen 32-octet nonces. Replay attacks during active sessions are mitigated via strict monotonic enforcement of the 64-bit Packet Number and a 64-packet sliding anti-replay window. Duplicate or out-of-window datagrams MUST be silently dropped.

section.name: IANA Considerations
section.t: This document requests the assignment of a UDP port for OTS and registration of the "ots" ALPN protocol identifier.
